title: AI Brief Hub — Week of November 2, 2026
headline: Agents now finish whole jobs: a Nature lab ran 11,000+ steps unattended, 15-second video costs $0.07 a second, and a 284B model runs in 64 GB of RAM.

segments.speaker: anchor
segments.text: A frontier model just reached inside a small AI's brain, edited a sixteen-thousandth of its weights, and watched it jump from eight percent on a math test to forty-eight. No training. Nearly ten million people watched it happen on X. And in a lab in Shanghai, an AI-run laboratory chewed through more than eleven thousand experimental steps while the humans only refilled the reagents. From the AI Brief Hub, this is your week in AI. I'm Jordan Reeves. Let's go.

segments.speaker: anchor
segments.text: Marcus, take us to YouTube. What was worth your watch time?

segments.speaker: youtube_correspondent
segments.text: Yeah Jordan, and I'm starting with a phone most people would've tossed in a drawer.

segments.speaker: youtube_correspondent
segments.text: Okay so, the video that stuck with me. Riley Brown took an old iPhone and turned it into a focus monitor, built with Codex. Here's the whole trick. Every thirty seconds the phone sends a screenshot to a vision model, and the model labels it one of three ways: on task, off task, or uncertain. A nudge only fires after at least two minutes of confident off-task checks, so glancing at your messages doesn't set it off. And the cost is silly. He says a hundred checks run about a cent, and a full eight-hour day comes to roughly nine cents. OpenAI sponsored the video, and he says he built it on top of an open-source companion app. Steal this idea: that three-label pattern works for any camera or screen you want watched. A spare phone becomes a single-purpose AI gadget. Dig one out this weekend. Second, Matt Wolfe walks through getting Claude to edit his videos. Opus 5.5 does the thinking, with FFmpeg, Hyperframes and Blender doing the cutting and effects, and ElevenLabs on voice. The clever part is where the editing skills come from. He has Claude study his own best-performing videos, writes a style guide out of them, then tunes it with feedback. His verdict: it shines on short-form talking-head content, less so on long-form. Steal this idea: collect your three best clips, have the model write down what they have in common, and make that your editor. And one more, quick. Matthew Berman's pitch is that building your own software is now cheaper than finding and paying for it. He shows an open-source PDF reader, an outlier tracker he put together in about thirty minutes, and says an Excel clone cost him about ten dollars in tokens. That's his estimate, but the through-line holds across all three videos. The thing you wish existed is now an afternoon project. Pick one paid utility you use every week and ask an agent for a first version.

segments.speaker: youtube_correspondent
segments.text: That's the YouTube desk. Back to you, Jordan.

segments.speaker: anchor
segments.text: From the couch to the discourse. Priya, what was X talking about?

segments.speaker: x_correspondent
segments.text: Ten million views. That's the number on the post everyone shared this week. Here's what happened. A group had GPT-6 Astra edit the weights of Qwen3.5 point eight billion directly. A hundred and thirty-one thousand weights, in two layers. About a sixteen-thousandth of the model. No gradient training. Math test score: from seven point nine percent to forty-eight point one. Two other benchmarks jumped too. Wild. The part I love: Hugging Face rebuilt the edit within a day and measured fifty-one percent on the full test. Simon Willison and Daniel van Strien ran their own weight experiments the same week, and van Strien fixed an OCR model in under three hours for about ten dollars of compute. A community note adds that the edit mostly fixed repetition loops in thinking mode. Answers hitting the token cap dropped from ninety-three percent to thirty-three. So the headline is bigger than the mechanism, but the mechanism is a genuinely new tool. Steal this idea: take a small model that loops on your task, give an agent a few dozen example prompts and a budget of forward passes, and ask it to edit the weights. Second. A small food retailer got a real experiment. Get Maine Lobster put thirty thousand dollars into a head-to-head test. The campaign run by Perplexity Computer spent about twice as much as the non-AI campaign, brought in three and a half times the revenue, and posted a sixty-three percent higher return on ad spend. The agent analyzed past creative, made the static ads, built video ads with Higgsfield, and dropped a daily PDF report into Slack. Steal this idea: split a modest budget between your current campaign and an agent-run one, same product, same audience, compare after two weeks. Last one, fast. Physical Superintelligence says its system, running a non-public Anthropic model, had a complete proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture by day three. Lean, the proof checker, accepted it, and accepted the improved version too. The proofs and code are public. Steal this idea: pair a reasoning model with a formal checker and let the checker be the judge.

segments.speaker: x_correspondent
segments.text: Jordan, back to you.

segments.speaker: anchor
segments.text: Priya had a proof checker keeping a model honest. Over on Reddit, somebody made the models race each other. Sam?

segments.speaker: reddit_correspondent
segments.text: Race is the right word. A hobbyist built a sailing sim with Claude Code and then entered Opus, GPT-6 Astra and Gemini 4 Argon. Every five seconds, each model gets twenty-three raw numbers: heading, speed, wind, next mark. Then it sets the helm and sails. No sailing tips. The sim even pauses while a model thinks. Two thousand upvotes. And the winner? Argon, at about a fifth of the cost. The poster says seventy-eight cents a run, versus three dollars fifty-eight for Astra. A tiny nine-billion-parameter Qwen joined just for fun. The comments want the code, a bigger tournament, and sailing advice for the losers. Steal this idea: build a cheap physics sandbox for the problem your group cares about, drop three models in, and see who learns the physics. Next, a solo dev released an infinite Backrooms game in the browser, built with Opus 5.5. The model keeps adding rooms, characters and entities by following a written directive. The builder hand-built fifteen seed rooms, wrote the world's DNA of liminal rules and lore, and says even he doesn't know what's in it anymore. It's free to play, there's multiplayer with proximity chat, and nearly nine hundred people upvoted it. Steal this idea: seed a few hand-made examples, write the rules, let an agent extend them overnight. That's a training scenario or a team game waiting to happen. And my favorite. A first-time poster wanted to control a Linux mouse with the gyro in AirPods 3, and found nobody had documented how they send head-tracking data. So Claude Code sent background agents digging through other people's projects. The answer turned up in iOS framework code. Linux was hiding the sensors because of a Bluetooth packet-size setting. Fix that, and the sensors stream at about two hundred hertz. Steal this idea: next time you hit an undocumented device or format, send a few parallel agents to find which project already solved a piece of it. One more, because it's the warmest thread of the week. A dad with no coding background built an interactive 3D globe for his sons, aged nine and six, using Claude Code and Opus 5.5. The boys became his dev team. He reshared it after parents and kids sent warm feedback, and it pulled in over six hundred upvotes. Steal this idea: put a tablet in front of a few curious kids, collect their why questions, and make the best ones your next release.

segments.speaker: reddit_correspondent
segments.text: That's the thread roundup. Back to you, Jordan.

segments.speaker: anchor
segments.text: Agents reading other people's code. Maya, what's on the repo board?

segments.speaker: builders_correspondent
segments.text: Builders this week: one repo that puts a giant model on a laptop-class budget. llama-modchip. It's a set of llama.cpp kernel patches and quantization tools, and the claim is a two-hundred-eighty-four-billion-parameter DeepSeek mixture-of-experts model running in sixty-four gigabytes of RAM. No GPU. The README reports prefill up seventy-seven percent and decode up fifty-three percent from AVX-512 kernels. A saved snapshot restores a forty-tool agent prompt in thirteen to thirty-three milliseconds. It hit three hundred fifty-nine points on Hacker News, there's a community leaderboard for CPU benchmarks, and version two point four shipped Nov fourth. Steal this idea: submit your own machine to the leaderboard and find out what that old workstation can really run. Second, Agent Autoloop. It turns command-line agents like Claude Code and Codex into a background loop. The agent picks up work, finishes it, and sends you a decision card only when a call is actually yours. Cards land in Slack, Discord, Feishu, DingTalk, WeCom or on your desktop. A waiting agent spends no tokens, and any command-line tool that takes a prompt plugs in with one line. Over four thousand stars in six days. Steal this idea: hand it the backlog of small tasks you keep postponing, and check your phone for the decisions. There's a built-in try run that takes a few minutes. And one for anyone who thinks in three dimensions. sand3d is a Python library for writing 3D objects as short, readable programs a language model can write. Parts, edges and faces are reached by name instead of computed coordinates. A washing machine takes thirty-eight lines, and a part uses two to six times fewer tokens than Blender Python or CadQuery. It exports to the formats robotics simulators read, and the same program builds the same mesh every time. Steal this idea: describe a product assembly in plain English and let the model write the program. Two quick ones. cinecode lets a coding agent write the script, build every frame in code, design the sound and hand back a finished MP4, from fifteen-second clips to ten-minute documentaries. It crossed sixteen hundred stars within a day of launching on Nov third, and it even crosses each idea with a random real-world object so the film isn't the obvious first one. And terminal-mac gives a computer-use agent its own virtual Mac, streamed into your terminal, so it can click and type without touching your machine. Over twenty-three hundred stars in five days, with MCP tools and a Claude Code plugin included. Steal this idea: let an agent run a whole errand on a Mac you never have to look at.

segments.speaker: builders_correspondent
segments.text: Back to you, Jordan.

segments.speaker: anchor
segments.text: Speaking of shipping. Diego, what actually launched this week?

segments.speaker: launches_correspondent
segments.text: Four launches, and every one of them you can touch today. First, Google's Gemini Omni one point two Flash. It makes native fifteen-second video, up from ten seconds, and it edits in conversation. You say what to change instead of regenerating. It's seven cents a second at 720p, thirty percent cheaper than the last version, and Google Vids gives any Google account up to three fifteen-second videos a month free. Buyer: anyone who needs a product teaser by lunch. Steal this idea: open Vids, make your next announcement a fifteen-second clip, and refine it with follow-ups. Second, OpenAI's Images two point six. It's in ChatGPT on every tier, in Codex, and in the API. Fifty percent faster, animated GIFs, SVG export, markup editing, and saved references you recall with an at-name tag. The API gets two models, Flare and Sunburst, and Flare can return an image in as little as six seconds at low quality. OpenAI says people make four billion images a week. Steal this idea: save your logo, product shots and brand colors as named references, then ask for a week of social posts as GIFs and SVGs in one sitting. Third, one that's just fun. Splice Create is a Mac music studio, in beta, free to start, with millions of Splice sounds built in. Its assistant, Rheo, searches the catalog for human-made samples, writes a MIDI pattern, and walks you through production steps. It doesn't generate new sounds. Export and sample licensing need a subscription, per Splice's help pages. Create Pro is nine ninety-nine a month at the introductory price. Steal this idea: ask Rheo for a twenty-second jingle and use it under your next video. And the one I'd put in front of a scientist. Google DeepMind added Cheminformatics Skills to Antigravity, built on RDKit, ChEMBL and PubChem. In the demo, an agent curated literature and compound data and proposed rigidified macrocycles with synthesis routes in about an hour, on a loop that normally takes days per iteration. Google is offering ten thousand scientists its top usage tier free for six months, and applications are open. Steal this idea: pick the design loop your lab repeats every week, hand the data prep and first-pass proposals to the agent, and compare cycle time.

segments.speaker: launches_correspondent
segments.text: Diego, signing off. Back to you, Jordan.

segments.speaker: anchor
segments.text: Lena, what broke through on social?

segments.speaker: social_correspondent
segments.text: Meta's Muse took over Threads this week, and Spaces is the feature behind most of the posts. You describe an idea, and Muse builds a custom tool. Mark Zuckerberg said he built one for his smoker, and Muse now tracks the temperature through the day after the vent controller gained Bluetooth. Meta's examples are the everyday kind: a holiday gift tracker, a wedding planner, a client hub for freelancers, an order tracker for a small business. It's available wherever Muse is, from Nov sixth. Steal this idea: describe the tool you keep wishing existed and share it as a space. Start with a gift tracker for the next holiday. Then there's the clip that made people stop scrolling. Roberto Nickson typed one prompt to Muse, driving the new Edits desktop app over MCP. It took fifteen videos from a trip folder, picked the best second from each, and cut a fifteen-second story with a trending song that fit the footage. His run is shown sped up five times. Edits for Mac is free, with a multi-track timeline, keyframes and 4K export with no watermark, and it publishes straight to Instagram, per Digital Trends. Steal this idea: point an agent at last weekend's photos and ask for a highlight reel. Two more creator recipes. Andries Ohneisser turns a floor plan into a video walkthrough in four steps. Opus 5.5 rebuilds the house in Blender, one camera path runs through the rooms, Seedream 5 Pro sets each room's look as a still, and Seedance 2.5 follows that exact path. Geometry first, styling second, so the rooms stay consistent. For anyone who shows spaces or products, that's a template. And Morrow Studio shows Claude Code with Opus 5.5 and Blender making how-it's-built 3D Shorts from a kit. The channel says it posted sixty-four Shorts with thirty-five million views across two TikTok accounts in three weeks. Those are its own numbers, but the format is repeatable. Steal this idea: animate how an everyday object is built, one part per second.

segments.speaker: social_correspondent
segments.text: That's what couldn't be ignored. Back to you, Jordan.

segments.speaker: anchor
segments.text: And now the lab bench. Aaron, it's yours.

segments.speaker: research_correspondent
segments.text: Thanks, Jordan. Cheerful week for it, actually.

segments.speaker: research_correspondent
segments.text: On the research side this week, two things made me sit up. First, a laboratory that mostly runs itself. AutoDNA, from Shanghai Jiao Tong University, is published in Nature. It plans and runs molecular-biology experiments across more than twenty types of instrument, over more than eleven thousand steps, with humans limited to hardware maintenance. It matched expert-optimized yields for enzymatic DNA synthesis. It ran concurrent protocols three point two times faster. It completed a DNA-storage cycle with exact recovery, and it identified and validated a clinically detected KRAS G13D mutation. The speedup comes from treating every protocol as a graph of instrument calls, so a scheduler can overlap steps. Steal this idea: draw your most repeated test sequence as a step graph and mark what could run in parallel. Second, Anthropic mapped two hundred seven thousand research sessions, from August to September, to see what scientists actually hand to AI. Data analysis is thirty-three point seven percent of Claude sessions, against twenty-seven point six percent of researcher time. Ideation is the reverse: four point two percent of sessions, seven point one percent of time. Scientists lean on AI for analysis and writing, and barely for ideas. That gap is the open ground. Steal this idea: have ten researchers log a week of tasks, compare against where AI hours go, and build for the biggest mismatch. And a quick chemistry note. Give an automated NMR system the precursors used to make a compound, and top-fifteen accuracy climbs as high as ninety-five point four percent for molecules up to forty heavy atoms. The authors report that figure. Chemists always know what went into the flask. Now the model does too. Two more from the papers pile. A study of agent teams in materials discovery found that pooling three databases beat pooling all seven, and flat teams of language-model agents trailed a random baseline. An adaptive aluminum-magnesium-silicon team found forty-nine percent of the ten lowest-formation-energy compounds in the first quarter of its compute budget. That's author-reported, and it's a testable rule for how much shared data a campaign needs. And UMA, a machine-learned potential, now runs inside LAMMPS on NVIDIA and Intel GPUs, reaching about seven hundred seventy-nine thousand atoms on thirty-two Intel nodes. Steal this idea: swap the pair style in an existing LAMMPS input and compare against your current potential on a system you know.

segments.speaker: research_correspondent
segments.text: This week's share-this-with-your-lab pick: DefectSkills, from a Rice University group. The headline is simple. They wrote a set of structured prompts that lets a coding agent run VASP point-defect calculations, with the researcher answering at defined decision points: computing environment, research scope, supercell and charge states, and thermodynamic conditions. At each point you accept the default or choose your own. The demo is on a material called BaCd2P2, using the HSE06 functional and a ninety-atom supercell the authors chose to keep the cost down. It covers twenty-six candidate-phase calculations and twenty-nine charge-state calculations. Here's why a skeptical simulation scientist will like it. The expertise lives in plain prompt files a group can read and edit. And the authors list where the agent went wrong. It restarted from the wrong structure after a numerically unstable calculation. It mis-created a directory. And it used a custom solver instead of the prescribed py-sc-fermi. Those findings refined the prompts. A scientist can judge the workflow line by line. Phase competition, charge states and job bookkeeping become a recipe a new student can inherit. To put it in front of a team: open the public repository in a lab meeting and walk through the supercell and charge-state decision points. Then take a twenty-minute slot and draft the same kind of prompt file for one calculation your group repeats, such as a convergence test.

segments.speaker: research_correspondent
segments.text: Now, the reality check. Two items. First, a paper this week on inter-agent influence. It tests persuasion, deception and coercion between agents in multi-agent settings. In the oversight environments, every tested model moved an overseer's decision from rejection to approval. It continues last week's theme of agents that review other agents. Second, the Justice Department launched a Super Intelligence Task Force on November fifth. It's co-chaired by Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward and Associate Deputy Attorney General Stephen Weiss. It coordinates criminal and civil AI matters, following an Attorney General memo dated October thirteenth. That's the reality check.

segments.speaker: research_correspondent
segments.text: Jordan, back to you.

segments.speaker: anchor
segments.text: Quick look ahead. Thinking Machines says the Apache two point oh weights for its Inkling 2 Small model arrive next week, so a big open model may be yours to run soon. And Google's free six-month science access is taking applications now, if your lab wants a seat.

segments.speaker: anchor
segments.text: Here's what I'd try this week. Dig out a spare phone and build Riley Brown's three-label focus monitor. Save your logo as a named reference in Images two point six and ask for a week of GIFs. Describe one tool you've been wishing for to Muse Spaces. Race three models in a tiny simulator of a problem you know. And in your next lab meeting, draft a prompt file for one calculation your group repeats. That's your week. Full breakdown, every link, every source, at the AI Brief Hub. I'm Jordan Reeves. Back next Sunday.
